main.text: [III, 289] [col. 464] Chapter IV.
What Joel says about locusts in his first chapter.

So far concerning the Egyptian locusts. With locusts like these the prophet Joel threatened the Israelites in the gravest terms, but at last he ends in words of peace and in God's name promises them many good things. It is therefore our task to pick out from Joel whatever he says about locusts and to interpret it as best we can, as each passage occurs and keeping to the Prophet's order. To capture attention, he declares at the very outset that he is about to say things new and unheard of, ch. I, 2: Hear this, he says, you old men, and give ear, all you inhabitants of the land: Has this happened in your days, or in the days of your fathers? First he addresses the old men, who by the benefit of age had seen and heard more. So Moses, Deut. XXXII, 7: Ask the old men, and they will tell you. And Job XXXII, 7: Days will speak, and the multitude of years will teach wisdom. The Prophet therefore signifies that the locusts of which he is about to speak wrought such destruction as none recorded in any age. In Judaea, that is. For this is the point of Hear this, you old men; and give ear, all you inhabitants of the land: supply [col. 465] of Judaea, which is the subject here. Likewise, when we read of the Egyptians in Exod. X, 14, Before them there were no such locusts as these, nor shall there be after them, this must be restricted to Egypt. Otherwise Moses would conflict with Joel, or Joel with Moses. For the other explanations which the Hebrews offer are less to the point, as we shall show below.
In the third verse, Tell this to your children, and your children to their children, and their children to another generation] Which you might express in the words of the Poet:
And the children's children, and those who shall be born of them.

For God's remarkable deeds must not be buried in oblivion; their memory must be diligently passed on to posterity and preserved for the future. Thus we may either be grateful and full of confidence for benefits received, or more fearful and cautious because of punishments inflicted. Hence David, Psal. LXXVIII, 3. etc.: What we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us, we will not hide from their children, another generation, so that they may tell the praises of the Lord, and his might, and the wonders that he has done, etc. And he commanded our fathers to make them known to their children, so that another generation might know, the children yet to be born, and that they might arise and tell them to their children. And that they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, etc. See also Deut. IV, 9. and VI, 6. 20. Ios. IV, 6. etc.

In the fourth verse, What the gazam left, the arbe has eaten, and what the arbe left, the jelek has eaten, and what the jelek left, the chasil has eaten.] These are four species of locusts, as [III, 290] we noted earlier ^{a)}, which we call here by their Hebrew names because Latin ones are not available. So too below, in chapter 2, verse 25: And I will restore to you the years which the ARBE, IELEK, CHASIL and GAZAM have eaten. There gazam, which had been first, is named last. This should be noted against the Hebrews, who think that these four species of locusts laid waste Judaea in four successive years: the gazam in the first year, the arbe in the second, the jelek in the third, and finally the chasil in the fourth. To me this seems hardly probable. For if the locust called gazam had been sent into Judaea in the first year, it would not be placed last in Ioel II, 25. And in enumerating these plagues the Prophet would have kept the same order in both places. Moreover, if each species had been assigned to a single year, it would not be said that the arbe ate what the gazam left, and the jelek what the arbe left, and the chasil what the jelek left. For this year's produce is not the remainder of the previous year's, nor can what will grow in the coming year be counted among this year's remains. Therefore, whether this plague of locusts lasted one year or, as seems rightly concluded from Ioel II, 25., extended over several years, I think that the individual species of locusts are not to be assigned to individual years, but that all of them fell upon Judaea in the same year. Thus, as one swarm left a field, another followed, to graze off and consume the remains of the preceding one, if any were left; and this was repeated as often as necessary, until nothing at all remained in the field on which either men or beasts could feed. Nor do I any more approve of their claim that this Judaean plague differed from the Egyptian in that a single kind of locust (namely ארבה arbe) fell upon Egypt, but those four species upon Judaea. For although arbe is taken εἰδικῶς [eidikōs] for a particular species of locust when it is set against the others, as in Joel and Levit. XI, 21., yet it is mostly used γενικῶς [genikōs] for the whole genus of locusts. So Moses took it when he dealt with the arbe sent upon the Egyptians, so that ילק jelek and חסיל chasil and other species of locusts were also included. Accordingly David says of the Egyptians, Psal. LXXVIII, 46.: He gave their produce to the chasil, and their labour to the arbe. And Psal. CV, 34.: He spoke, and the arbe came, and the jelek without number. Thus not the arbe alone, but also the chasil and the jelek were sent by God against them. Rightly, then, in Pisides God arrays against the Egyptians παγγενῆ τὴν ἀκρίδα [pangenē tēn akrida], the locust of every kind. How the Chaldeans, Syrians and Arabs render the four species of locusts in Joel, gazam, arbe, jelek and chasil, [col. 466] is of no concern here. In the Greek and the Vulgate they are ἡ κάμπη [hē kampē], ἡ ἀκρὶς [hē akris], ὁ βροῦχος [ho brouchos], ἡ ἐρυσίβη [hē erysibē]: eruca [caterpillar], locusta [locust], bruchus [bruchus], rubigo [blight]. Of these the first and the last do not belong to the genus of locusts. For ἡ ἐρυσίβη [hē erysibē], rubigo [blight], is not even an animal, but a disease of crops. We therefore by no means stand by this version. For we are fully persuaded [III, 291] that the four Hebrew words signify four species of locusts. This all the Hebrews assert here with one voice, although they cannot define how those species differ from one another.

But whatever these words may mean, a serious question is raised, namely, whether what is said here about locusts is to be explained literally. For many look for mysteries here, as though not real locusts were meant but the enemies of the Jews. Jerome seems to waver between the two opinions in such a way that he leans more towards the latter. For first he refers these things to the four empires which one after another rose up against the Jews. "The caterpillar," he says, "which in Hebrew is called גזם gazam, in Greek κάμπη [kampē], the Hebrews interpret as the Assyrians, the Babylonians and Chaldeans; who, coming from one region of the world, laid waste everything of the ten tribes as well as of the two, that is, of the Israelite people. The locust they interpret as the Medes and Persians; who, after overthrowing the empire of the Chaldeans, held the Jews captive. The bruchus as the Macedonians and all the successors of Alexander, and above all King Antiochus, surnamed Epiphanes, who settled in Judaea like a bruchus and devoured all the remains left by the earlier kings. The blight they refer to the Roman empire; who, fourth and last, so oppressed the Jews as to drive them from their own territory." So he writes, as if from the mind of the Hebrews, who nevertheless, by his own admission, acknowledge that what is said here about locusts also happened literally. "The Jews," he says, "think that in the days of Joel so countless a multitude of locusts came upon Judaea that they filled everything; and left, I will not say the crops, but not even the bark and branches of the vines and trees." But he refutes this opinion of the Jews in what follows: "Whether this happened or not, we cannot clearly affirm. For the history of the Kings and Chronicles does not narrate it. And if it had happened, Scripture would certainly never have kept silent. We say only that under the metaphor of locusts the coming of enemies is described." Then, as if undecided between the two opinions: "If I am not mistaken," he says, "I seem to have found something in this Prophet. The impiety of the enemies is narrated under the figure of locusts. And again, the locusts themselves are spoken of as if they were compared to enemies: so that when you read of locusts you think of enemies; when you have thought of enemies, you return to the locusts." Cyril seems to agree with Jerome, understanding by these four plagues Shalmaneser, Nebuchadnezzar, Antiochus and the Romans. Yet in the same author you may read this: Ἀληθὲς μὲν οὖν τὸ χρῆμα, κἂν εἰ ἐπὶ ἀκρίδος τυχὸν νοοῖτο, βρούχου τε, καὶ κάμπης· [Alēthes men oun to chrēma, kan ei epi akridos tychon nooito, brouchou te, kai kampēs] "This is indeed true, even if it be taken of the locust, the bruchus and the caterpillar." Theodoret, after writing that some interpret these things figuratively of four kings of Assyria, Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar, says: Ἐγὼ δὲ ἀληθῆ μὲν ἡγοῦμαι καὶ ταῦτα· ὑπολαμβάνω δὲ καὶ τὰ κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν νοούμενα τῷ ὄντι γεγενῆσθαι· [Egō de alēthē men hēgoumai kai tauta; hypolambanō de kai ta kata to rhēton nooumena tō onti gegenēsthai] "I indeed consider these things true; [III, 292] but I also think that what is understood literally really happened." The Chaldee mostly embraces the literal sense. Sometimes, however, he slips into the mystical: as in Ioel. II, 25., where for the four kinds of locusts, arbe, jelek, chasil and gazam, he has עממיא ולשניא ושלטוניא ומלכותא פרענות, "peoples, and tongues, and dominions, and kingdoms of vengeance"; that is, those whom God used to take vengeance on the rebels among his people. Of the Hebrew commentators, Jarchi, Kimchi and Aben Ezra cling tenaciously to the letter. But Abarbanel, later than these, following Jerome, [col. 467] asserts that this Prophet came להתנבאות על ממשלת ארבע המלכיות בבל ופרס ויון ורומי, "to prophesy concerning the dominion of the four empires, namely the Babylonian, and the Persian, and the Greek, and the Roman." And he is so averse to the literal sense that, dealing with those who refer these things to locusts, he exclaims in the very preface: חלילה לי מלהאמין בזה, "Far be it from me to believe this", as though it were utterly absurd. But since he objects nothing that is not most futile, I do not doubt that real locusts are meant by the Prophet, which laid waste Judaea shortly after his prophecy. For hostile enemies are not usually compared with locusts except in respect of number: as when it is said of the Midianites and Amalekites, Iud. VI, 5., "They came like locusts in multitude." And Iud. VII, 12., "They were spread out in that valley like locusts in multitude." And Iudith. II, 2., of the forces of the Assyrians: "And many of mixed stock, like locusts, gathered to them." And of the Trojans and the Ethiopians whom Memnon had brought, Quintus Smyrnaeus, book 2, line 195.

— — — — τοί δ' ἐκέχυντο Ἀκρίσι καρποβόροις ἐναλίγκιοι, αἵ τε φέρονται Ὡς νέφος, ἢ πολὺς ὄμβρος ὑπὲρ χθονὸς εὐρυπέδοιο, Ἄπλητοι, μερόπεσσιν ἀεικέα λοιμὸν ἄγουσαι· [— — — — toi d' ekechynto Akrisi karpoborois enalinkioi, hai te pherontai Hōs nephos, ē polys ombros hyper chthonos eurypedoio, Aplētoi, meropessin aeikea loimon agousai]

But they poured themselves forth, like crop-devouring locusts, which are borne along like a cloud, or a heavy rain over the broad earth, countless, bringing a dreadful famine upon men. For otherwise, when men are compared to locusts, this serves to express contempt, and πρὸς τὸν ἐξουθενισμόν [pros ton exouthenismon]. Such is the statement about the Israelites when compared with the Anakim giants, Num. XIII, 34. Compared with them we seemed like locusts. And about men in comparison with God, Es. XL, 22. He who sits upon the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like locusts. Not unlike this is Lucian's phrase in the Hermotimus, Οἷον μύρμηκας ἀπὸ τοῦ ὕψους ἐπισκοποῦντάς τινας τοὺς ἄλλους [Hoion myrmēkas apo tou hypsous episkopountas tinas tous allous], Looking down from on high upon other men as if upon ants. Thus you will nowhere see great empires compared with these little animals, but rather with lions, leopards and bears, as in the seventh chapter of Daniel. But to make the matter clearer, let us now examine what follows.
In verse 5, Awake, you drunkards (for whom long drinking usually brings on sleep, [III, 293] — — and from the wine sense returns to their breasts,

as we read in the Poet); weep and wail, all you drinkers of wine, because of the new wine; for it is cut off from your mouth] As below in verse 9, The sacrifice is cut off. And in verse 16, Before our eyes the food is cut off. Namely by the locusts, one species of which is called גזם gazam from cutting off. But the Prophet here uses the verb כרת, as in Nahum III, 15. תכריתך, the sword shall cut you off, and shall consume you like the bruchus.

In verse 6, For a nation has come up against my land, strong and without number. Its teeth are like the teeth of a lion, and its molars like those of a lioness.] On which Abarbanel says, לא אמר הנביא זה באמת על הארבה כי איך יקראהו גוי וקהל גוים, The Prophet certainly did not say this of the locusts: for how could he call them a nation, and an assembly of nations? But the Prophet had someone to follow, the wisest of kings, whose words are Prov. XXX, 25. 26. הנמלים עם לא עז, The ants, a people not strong. And, שפנים עם לא עצום, The choerogrylli, a people not mighty. For what he cites there from the Midrash is ridiculous, namely that in that passage too Solomon signified four empires by the four little animals. I admit, indeed, that the word nation is properly used of man, and is not transferred to beasts except by metaphor. But nothing is more common than that metaphor. Hence the most ancient of poets, and also the best, said in Iliad β´, verse 87,
Ἠΰτε ἔθνεα εἶσι μελισσάων ἁδινάων, [Ēute ethnea eisi melissaōn hadinaōn]
As go the nations of thronging bees. Where the Scholiast says, Πρώτη δὲ αὕτη παραβολὴ τῷ ποιητῇ· [Prōtē de hautē parabolē tō poiētē]. And verse 458,
— — ὀρνίθων πετεηνῶν ἔθνεα πολλὰ, Χηνῶν, ἢ γεράνων, ἢ κύκνων δουλιχοδείρων. [— — ornithōn peteēnōn ethnea polla, Chēnōn, ē geranōn, ē kyknōn doulichodeirōn]
Many nations of winged birds, of geese, or cranes, or long-necked swans. [col. 468] And verse 469,
Ἠΰτε μυιάων ἁδινάων ἔθνεα πολλὰ, [Ēute myiaōn hadinaōn ethnea polla]
As the many nations of thronging flies. And Odyssey ξ, verse 73, of the pigsties,
— — — ἔνθ᾽ ἔθνεα ἔρχατο χοίρων, [— — — enth' ethnea erchato choirōn]
Where the nations of swine were penned. And Orpheus, On Stones, in the section on Coral,
Ἔκ τε μύων ἀγέλας, ἐκ τ᾽ ἀκρίδος ἄπλετον ἔθνος Ῥαίσει. — — — — — [Ek te myōn agelas, ek t' akridos apleton ethnos Rhaisei. — — — — —]

And it will destroy the herds of mice, and the boundless nation of locusts. Oppian also, near the beginning of book 3 of the Cynegetica, [III, 294] Ἀλλ᾽ ὅτε δὴ κεραῶν ἠείσαμεν ἔθνεα θήρων, [All' hote dē keraōn ēeisamen ethnea thērōn]
But after we have sung the nations of horned beasts. And Lucillius, book 2 of the Anthology, chapter 26,
Ὄψει καὶ γυπῶν ἔθνεα, καὶ κοράκων· [Opsei kai gypōn ethnea, kai korakōn]
You will see nations of both vultures and ravens. And Pisides in the Hexaemeron,
Τίς ἐκστρατεύει παγγενῆ τὴν ἀκρίδα, Ἔθνος πτερωτὸν, εἰς φθορὰν Αἰγυπτίων; [Tis ekstrateuei pangenē tēn akrida, Ethnos pterōton, eis phthoran Aigyptiōn?]
Who marshals the locust of every kind, a winged nation, for the destruction of the Egyptians? Nor do the Latin writers speak otherwise. As when the Poet says of horses in book 3 of the Georgics,
Only those whom you shall choose to rear for the hope of the race [gentis].
And of calves,
— — they brand on them marks and the names of the race [gentis].
Such too is the passage in the same place where the plague seizes
The hope and the flock together, and the whole race [gentem] from its origin:
that is, the whole fold. As when in book 4 the fish of Proteus are called
— — the watery nation [gens] of the vast sea.
And of bees the same poet in the same place,
— — — and of the whole nation [gentis] in order I shall tell the customs, and pursuits, and peoples, and battles.
And again,
As the kings have two aspects, so do the bodies of the nation [gentis].
And in book 1 of the Aeneid,
— — when they lead forth the full-grown young of the nation [gentis].

Lest anyone think this manner of speaking peculiar to the poets, it also occurs in Columella, book 10, chapter 3: The whole nation of an entire hive is consumed. And in chapter 9: Whole nations (of bees) are consumed by civil war. And in chapter 10, of the king of the bees whose wings have been removed: He does not even allow the people of his own dominion to roam farther. And in chapter 13: Two peoples must be joined. And of the drones, in chapter 15: Nor is the nation to be destroyed to the point of extermination. Similar is what Aelian, book 6 of the History, chapter 19, called τὸ τεττίγων φῦλον [to tettigōn phylon], the nation of cicadas. For so he had written, not φῶλον [phōlon], a meaningless word, which [III, 295] our editions have. Moreover, the Arabic lexicographers Giauhari and Alcamus note that in Arabic too أمة [umma] umma, nation, is said of any animal. So in the celebrated saying of the pseudo-prophet about the animals, which we cited above ^{b)}: خلق الله الف امة منها ستماية في البحر واربعماية في البر وان اول هلاك هذه الامم الجراد [khalaqa Allāh alf umma minhā sittumiʾa fī al-baḥr wa-arbaʿumiʾa fī al-barr wa-inna awwal halāk hādhihi al-umam al-jarād] God created a thousand nations of animals (so it reads word for word), six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land. And the first plague of these nations is the locust. Why then should Joel not have called the locusts here גוי, a nation, and עם, a people, in chapter 2, verse 2?

To them are assigned the teeth and molars of lions, as in Apoc. IX, 8. Ὀδόντες αὐτῶν ὡς λεόντων ἦσαν [Odontes autōn hōs leontōn ēsan], Their teeth were as those of lions, that is, hard, strong, sharp. Accordingly Pliny says of locusts: Gnawing everything with their bite, even the doors of houses. This strength is truly astonishing in so paltry a little creature. So not without reason does Jerome exclaim at these words: What is stronger than locusts, which human industry cannot resist? And Cyril: Ἄμαχον τὸ χρῆμά ἐστι, καὶ ἀκαταγώνιστος κομιδῆ τῶν τοιούτων ἡ ἔφοδος, ἱκανή τε ἄρδην ἀπολέσαι τὰ ἐν ἀγροῖς. [Amachon to chrēma esti, kai akatagōnistos komidē tōn toioutōn hē ephodos, hikanē te ardēn apolesai ta en agrois.] [col. 469] The thing is invincible; their onset is utterly irresistible and fully capable of destroying the wealth of the countryside. What they have bitten off the Arabs call تاشر [tāshur], that is, toothed like a saw. For اشر [ashara] means to cut with a saw ^{(1)}.

Verse 7: He has laid my vine waste, and my fig tree broken. He has stripped it bare and cast it away; its branches are made white.] He says vine and fig tree, because bruchi and locusts are harmful to both. Accordingly, to keep bruchi away from vines, Didymus prescribes this in book 10 of the Geoponica: Περὶ τὸ στέλεχος τῆς ἀμπέλου παρὰ τὴν ῥίζαν, τρεῖς κόκκους σινήπεως χῶσον· φυτευόμενα γὰρ ταῦτα τῇ ὀσμῇ τὸν βροῦχον ἀναιρεῖ. [Peri to stelechos tēs ampelou para tēn rhizan, treis kokkous sinēpeōs chōson; phyteuomena gar tauta tē osmē ton brouchon anairei.] Bury three grains of mustard around the trunk of the vine at the root: for when planted they kill the bruchus by their smell. And of fig trees Pliny, book 17, chapter 25: In Boeotia fig trees gnawed by locusts sprouted again. This is taken from these words of Theophrastus, book 2 of the History, chapter 4: Ἐν δὲ τῇ Βοιωτίᾳ καταβρωθέντων τῶν ἔργων ὑπὸ τῶν ἀττελέβων πάλιν ἀνεβλάστησε. [En de tē Boiōtia katabrōthentōn tōn ergōn hypo tōn attelebōn palin aneblastēse.] Therefore instead of τῶν ἔργων [tōn ergōn] one should read τῶν ἐρίνων [tōn erinōn]. For ἔρινα [erina] are wild figs, or any unripe figs, as [III, 296] in Alexis in Athenaeus. I render the Hebrew לקצפה into breaking, with the Greeks, who here have εἰς κλασμὸν [eis klasmon] or συγκλασμόν [synklasmon] ^{(2)}. This rendering of a word otherwise unusual is confirmed from Arabic usage. For in Arabic قصف [qaṣafa] means to break, and القصيف [al-qaṣīf] is a broken branch of a tree. So Giauhari and Ibno-maruph. This is very much to the point, provided it is referred to the topmost branches of trees, on which locusts feed. Hence some think they are called ἀκρίδες [akrides], παρὰ τὸ ἄκρας τῶν ἀσταχύων καὶ τῶν φυτῶν νέμεσθαι [para to akras tōn astachyōn kai tōn phytōn nemesthai]. For Jerome קצפה is decortication. Accordingly he has here, He has stripped the bark from my fig tree. And more than once he writes that trees are stripped of bark by locusts. So on Hosea chapter 13: The locust is so harmful that it strips the bark even from trees and vines. And on Joel: the Jews think that in the days of Joel so innumerable a multitude of locusts came that they did not spare even the bark and branches of the vines and trees. And below: Locusts lay everything waste to such a degree that they gnaw away the bark of trees. The Chaldee, who rendered the word קצפה quite differently, nevertheless concluded that trees are stripped of bark by locusts from what follows about the fig tree, חשף חשפה, stripping he has stripped it, which he interprets thus: מקלף קלף, barking he has barked it. But for a tree to be said to be stripped, it is not necessary that its bark be removed. It suffices that the leaves and fruit, or flowers, be taken away. Hence the old Poet in the Description of the Four Seasons of the Year:
Winter strips the grove of its leaves, and the rivers grow stiff.

In Greek you would call this ψιλοῦν [psiloun]. Theophrastus, Historia Plantarum, book 4, chapter 16: Ἐν Μιλήτῳ δὲ τὰς ἐλαίας, ὅταν ὦσι περὶ τὸ ἀνθεῖν, κάμπαι κατεσθίουσιν; αἱ μὲν τὰ φύλλα, αἱ δὲ τὰ ἄνθη ἕτεραι τῷ γένει· καὶ ψιλοῦσι τὰ δένδρα [En Milētō de tas elaias, hotan ōsi peri to anthein, kampai katesthiousin; hai men ta phylla, hai de ta anthē heterai tō genei; kai psilousi ta dendra]. At Miletus caterpillars gnaw the olives when they are in flower, some the leaves, others, of a different kind, the flower, and so they strip the trees bare. But in Joel it follows that the branches of the fig tree turn white. It will seem that this cannot happen unless the bark is stripped off so that the sapwood is exposed, as was done by Jacob, Gen. XXX, 37. I reply that the bark of a tree itself turns white when it rots. Hence Theophrastus, De causis, book 5, chapter 12: Διὰ τὴν ἀτροφίαν ἐκλευκαίνεται καὶ ἀπόλλυται τὰ δένδρα [Dia tēn atrophian ekleukainetai kai apollytai ta dendra]; For lack of nourishment trees turn white and perish. That trees perish and wither at the touch of locusts will be shown below. However that may be, it is established from the histories of the Abyssinians that locusts cut off not only the bark but even the stems of shrubs, when they are reduced to a lack of other fodder ^{(3)}. So Scaliger asserts in the 192nd Exercitatio against Cardano.

[III, 297] Verse 9: The meal offering and the drink offering are cut off from the house of the Lord; the priests, the ministers of the Lord, mourn. [col. 470]] As in verse 13: Come, and spend the night in sackcloth; for the meal offering and the drink offering are withheld from the house of your God. From both these passages Abarbanel infers that the temple had then been destroyed by the Babylonians; whereas the contrary follows, namely that the temple was standing. For a sacrifice cannot be cut off or withheld from a house that no longer exists.

Verse 10: The field is laid waste, the land mourns; for the grain is laid waste, the new wine has blushed, the oil languishes.] From these the firstfruits and tithes were offered to the Lord, Num. XVIII, 12. Deut. XIV, 23. and XVIII, 3. 4. And from the same the meal offerings and drink offerings were made. So when these three were lacking, there was nothing from which the customary oblations could be made. The land is said to mourn, as among the Hebrews is said of whatever has been laid waste and made desolate and changed for the worse. So Es. XXIV, 7: The new wine mourns, the vine languishes. Thren. II, 8: He made the rampart and the wall mourn; they languished together. By the same figure the oil is said to languish and the new wine to blush (as the vine in verse 12), as though affected with shame because they cannot meet the expectation of men. Thus Es. XXXIII, 9: The land mourned and languished, Lebanon blushed. To the mourning land is opposed a field glad with crops and fodder in Sallust, Histories, book 2, and glad crops in the Poet. Hence too the dung with which fields are manured is commonly called laetamen, as Servius writes, which in Italian is letame.

Verse 11: Be ashamed, O farmers; wail, O vinedressers, for the wheat and the barley; because the harvest of the field has perished. 12. The vine has blushed, etc.] The order would be: "Be ashamed, O farmers, for the wheat and the barley, because the harvest of the field has perished. Wail, O vinedressers, because the vine has blushed." But these are transposed by a figure such as the χιασμός [chiasmos]. Such is that said of the church, Cant. I, 4. (var. 5.): I am black, but comely, as the tents of Kedar, and the curtains of Solomon. That is, "Outwardly, and in the [III, 298] judgement of men, I am black, like the haircloth tents of the Kedarenes; but comely inwardly, and before God, like the magnificent curtains of Solomon." So there is a like μετάθεσις [metathesis].

Verse 12: The vine has blushed, and the fig tree languishes. The pomegranate too, the palm, and the apple tree, all the trees of the field have withered, because joy has perished from the sons of men. That is, the joy they feel at harvest and vintage, and when the fruits of the trees are gathered. Hence Es. IX, 3: They have rejoiced before you with the joy that is at harvest. And Psal. IV, 8: You have put greater gladness in my heart than at the time when their grain and new wine abounded. Although it is plain that these verses concern the damage inflicted by locusts on the crops of the land and the fruits of the trees, Abarbanel nevertheless found something to object. Namely, that if the matter concerned locusts, it would be pointless to say that the vine, the fig tree and all the trees of the field had withered, since locusts consume the fruit but do not harm the trees themselves in the least. From this it is clear that this plague was little known to him. For Pliny writes that the locust scorches many things by its touch. And Pisides in the Creation of the World:
Τήκει τὰ δένδρα, καὶ μαραίνει τὴν πόαν, [Tēkei ta dendra, kai marainei tēn poan,]

It makes trees waste away and renders the grass withered. And Damir: لعابه سم ناقع النبات والشجر لا يقع علي شي منه الا اهلكه [luʿābuhu samm nāqiʿ al-nabāt wa-l-shajar lā yaqaʿu ʿalā shayʾ minhu illā ahlakahu], Its saliva is a most potent poison to plants and trees, so that whatever it falls upon, it destroys. Muffet, following Valeriola, reports the same thing in these words: They harm crops, pastures, meadows, gardens and orchards not only by their bite, but also by their dung, which is black, green, biting and heavy, and above all by their bilious and acrid saliva, which they pour from their mouths in quantity while gnawing.

In verse fifteen: Alas for that day! for the day of the Lord is near, and it shall come as devastation from the Almighty. The day of the Lord, that is, the day on which he will sit as [col. 471] judge to punish the Jews by sending the swarm of locusts against them. For learned men rightly observe that day is taken here for judgment. So in 1 Cor. IV, 3. With me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of man's day, that is, by human judgment. Jerome writes to Algasia, in Question 10, that this was how the Cilicians spoke, from whom Paul came. I would believe that they borrowed it from their neighbours the Syrians. As devastation from the Almighty] In Hebrew כשד משדי, an elegant paronomasia, as if someone were to say in Greek ὡς ἀπώλειαν ἀπ᾽ Ἀπόλλωνος [hōs apōleian ap᾽ Apollōnos], or ὡς δήωσιν ἐκ Δηοῦς [hōs dēōsin ek Dēous]. Yet the divine name שדי saddai does not mean devastator, but παντοκράτορα [pantokratora], almighty, just as in Arabic شد [shadda] sadda means to strengthen.

In verse sixteen: Is not the food cut off before our eyes, joy and gladness from the house of our God?] Hence it again appears that the subject is the temple while still standing, [III, 299] not as overthrown by the Chaldeans, as Abarbanel holds. By joy is meant the joy of those who cheerfully ate of the sacrifices and firstfruits offered in God's temple, as the Law commands, Deut. XII, 6. 7. Thither ye shall bring your burnt offerings, and your sacrifices, and your tithes, and the offerings of your hand, etc. That there, eating before the Lord your God, ye may rejoice, ye and your households, etc. And Deut. XVI, 10. 11. Thou shalt keep the feast of weeks unto the Lord thy God with a freewill offering, etc. And thou shalt rejoice before the Lord thy God. And 1 Paralip. XIX, 21. 22. They sacrificed unto the Lord, etc. And they did eat and drink before the Lord on that day with great gladness. So, when Alcinous offers sacrifice to Jupiter, Odyssey book 3, the Phaeacians
Μηρὰ δὲ κήαντες δαίνυντ᾽, ἐρικυδέα δαῖτα Τερπόμενοι· — — — — — [Mēra de kēantes dainynt᾽, erikydea daita Terpomenoi]
Roasting the thighs, they feasted, delighting in a splendid banquet. But this joy ceases when offerings are lacking. And they were lacking, because the locusts had left nothing untouched.

In verse 17, The seeds have rotted under their clods, the storehouses are desolate, the granaries are destroyed, because the grain has withered.] In the first clause of this verse, עבשו פרדות תחת מגרפותיהם, three of the four words are found nowhere else. Hence the interpreters are at a loss here, and nowhere is there greater disagreement. For the Greeks render it Ἐσκίρτησαν δαμάλεις ἐπὶ ταῖς φάτναις [Eskirtēsan damaleis epi tais phatnais], The heifers have leapt at their mangers ^{(4)}. And Jerome: The beasts have rotted [III, 300] in their dung. And the Chaldee: אתמסיו גרבי חמר תחות מגופתהון, The jars of wine have run out under their lids ^{(5)}. And the Syriac again differently ^{(6)}. We, with the Hebrews: The seeds have rotted under their clods. That is, עבשׁו is the same as עפשׁו, with Beth and Pe interchanged, letters which are homogeneous and easily interchangeable. Further, in the Talmudists עפשׁ means to rot. So Jerome rightly has computruerunt [have rotted]. And that פרדות is truly to be explained as seeds is suggested by the fact that in Syriac ܦܪܕܬܐ is a seed. Hence in the Syriac version, Matth. XIII, 31, ܦܪܕܬܐ ܕܚܪܕܠܐ is a grain of mustard seed; Ioh. XII, 24, ܦܪܕܬܐ ܕܚܛܬܐ, a grain of wheat; 1 Corinth. XV, 37, ܦܪܕܬܐ ܕܚܛܬܐ ܘܕܣܥܪܐ, grains of wheat and of barley ^{(7)}. Finally, that מגרפות are clods [III, 301] is suggested by the similarity of the words גרף (whence מגרפות) and רגב, the latter of which occurs twice in Job for clod. And indeed clods seem to be called מגרפות from the verb גרף, which, used of a torrent, means to carry away. Thus Iud. V, 21: the torrent Kishon גרפם, swept them away. And in Arabic, in Alcamus: جرفته السيل [jarafathu al-sayl], the torrent swept him away; سيل جراف [sayl jurāf], a torrent sweeping everything away; جرف [jurf], a clod of earth which a torrent carries away. Thus מגרפות are properly רגבי נחל, clods of the torrent, as they are called in Iob. XXI, 33, and then also clods of any kind ^{(8)}. Further, grains (or seeds) [III, 302] usually rot under their clods (that is, when cast into the ground) when the [col. 472] rains are excessive. Hence Pliny, book 10, chapter 24, wants sowing in humid places [III, 303] to be done earlier, lest the seed rot from the rain. And Kimchi on this passage of Joel: יתעפשו גרגרי הזרע מפני הגשמים, The grains of seed rot because of the rains ^{(9)}. And Junius: The sown crops have become mouldy from excessive rains, which spoil the seed. In the same sense the distinguished Diodati: Accenni che le semente sarebbero guaste da soverchie piogge ^{(10)}. But this does not agree with what follows, where extreme drought is described. For this is what verse 19 refers to: Fire has consumed the pastures of the wilderness, and flame has scorched all the trees of the field. And verse 20: Even the beasts of the field cry to you, because the channels of water have dried up and fire has consumed the pastures of the wilderness. Fire and flame, that is, excessive heat. As in Psal. LXXXII, 13. (var. LXXXIII, 15.): As fire burns the forest, and flame sets the mountains ablaze. Hence places parched by the heat of the sun are called חררים in Ierem. XVII, 6., that is, burning or scorched. So the rotting of the sown crops of which Joel speaks comes not from rains but from extreme drought. By this, if we wish to speak properly, seeds are said not so much to rot as to come to nothing. Pliny, in the place cited above: The reason for sowing earlier in humid places is lest the seed rot from the rain; in dry places later, so that rains may follow, lest, lying long and not germinating, it come to nothing. Such is what he said in the preceding chapter, that harmful winds empty the grains. But whether the grains rot from rain or come to nothing from drought, the Hebrew עבש, or עבש, could cover both ^{(11)}. As in Hesiod's Shield the bones of corpses [III, 304] Σειρίου ἀζαλέοιο κελαινῇ πύθεται αἴῃ [Seiriou azaleoio kelainē pythetai aiē],

Under parching Sirius they rot in the black earth. As though drought too were a cause of rotting. And that very drought which the Prophet mentions was the reason why the locusts came forth more abundantly. For of them Pliny says thus in book 11, chapter 28: The eggs perish from spring rains; in a dry spring the yield is greater. And of the attelabi the Philosopher, book 5 of the History, chapter 29: Φθείρεται δὲ αὐτῶν τὰ ὠὰ ὑπὸ τῶν μετοπωρινῶν ὑδάτων, ὅταν πολλὰ γένηται. ἂν δὲ αὐχμὸς συμβῇ, τότε γίνονται μᾶλλον ἀττέλαβοι πολλοὶ, διὰ τὸ αὐτὰ μὴ φθείρεσθαι ὁμοίως. [Phtheiretai de autōn ta ōa hypo tōn metopōrinōn hydatōn, hotan polla genētai. an de auchmos symbē, tote ginontai mallon attelaboi polloi, dia to auta mē phtheiresthai homoiōs.] Their eggs are destroyed by autumn rains, if these are heavy. But in a dry autumn the yield of attelabi is larger, because then they are not destroyed in the same way. Hence Tertullian, On the Soul, chapter 32: Locusts, little butterflies and chameleons rejoice in droughts ^{(12)}. Therefore, so that the eggs of locusts may be destroyed, Moffett, following Valleriola and Peucer, teaches that at the beginning of spring torrents should be diverted into the places where they lie, so as to soak the whole surface of the ground, or the greater part of it, abundantly. So much for the first chapter of Joel; now to the second.

notes.text: That there is a certain likeness between the sharp, toothed jaws of locusts and the jaws of lions, which the prophet has in view in this comparison, is observed by C. Guil. Iusti in the notes appended to his vernacular translation of Joel, from Fabricius, Genera Insectorum, p. 96.
So also the Syriac, ܠܡܫܘܚܠܐ, for tearing apart, and the Arabic in the Polyglots, للتفسيخ [li-l-tafsīkh], for rending.

All this is confirmed by Shaw, Travels p. 165. 166, German trans., where he describes at length the devastation brought upon the regions of North Africa by locusts. Moreover, [III, 297] as regards the interpretation of the word שריגים, rendered by some branches, by others vine-shoots, I add the words of Ed. Pococke in his Commentary on Joel p. 34, Latin trans.: “Abu Walid compares this word with the Arabic root سرغ [s-r-gh], which is used of leaves and branches انا امتدت [anā imtaddat] when they stretch themselves out. The foremost lexicographer of the Arabs, the author of the Qamus (Firuzabadi), says that the noun سرغ [sargh] means قضب الكرم للغض لسنته [quḍub al-karm li-l-ghaḍḍ li-sanatihi], the tender little branches of the vine of the first year, or كل قضيب رطب [kull qaḍīb raṭb], any moist (or green) rod. He likewise tells us that السرغ [al-sargh] alsargo, joined with غ g (which in sound differs little from the Hebrew), is قضيب الكرم [qaḍīb al-karm], the rod (or branch) of the vine.”

That they rendered ἐσκίρτησαν [eskirtēsan], I think the reason was not that they read בעטו for עבשו, as Cappellus conjectured, Crit. S. vol. II, p. 631, Vogel-Scharfenberg edition (a conjecture in which he has a follower in I. D. Michaelis, Supplemm. vol. VI, p. 1825); nor פשו, having grown fat they behaved foolishly, as I. Fr. Fischer would have it in Proluss. de Verss. Graecc. Librr. V. T. p. 13; nor פשו, they leap, which seemed probable to Scharfenberg on Cappellus, loc. cit.; but rather that they took the Hebrew עבש in the sense of playing, which belongs to the Arabic عبث [ʿabath], which is the view of Ed. Pococke in his Commentary p. 84, Latin trans.; or that they compared עבש with أفز [afaza], to leap up, which is the less probable opinion of Boysen, in a book written in the vernacular entitled Beyträge zu einem richtigen System der Hebräischen Philologie, vol. I, p. 342. That the Alexandrian and the Syriac translators read פרות in their manuscripts instead of פרדות, Mercerus, Cappellus, Fischer, Michaelis and others infer from the fact that the former put δαμάλεις [damaleis], the latter ܥܓ̈ܠܐ, calves. To these they also add the Latin Vulgate, which renders jumenta [beasts of burden], although to some it seems to have read the word with the same consonants but not the same vowels: as if it had formed a plural from פרדה, the feminine of the noun פרד, mule; one kind of beast being named, under which the other beasts of similar nature, or young animals in general, are included. Finally, Fischer concludes that instead of what we read today, מגרפתיהם, the Greek Alexandrian translator [III, 300] found in his manuscript הרפתיהם, from the fact that he rendered ἐπὶ ταῖς φάτναις αὐτῶν [epi tais phatnais autōn]; and רפתים is in another passage too (Habac. III, 17.) called φάτναι [phatnai] by the same translators. Mercerus, however, in his commentary on this passage, thinks that both this Greek rendering, ἐπὶ ταῖς φάτναις αὐτῶν [epi tais phatnais autōn], at their mangers or in their stalls, and the Latin Vulgate, in stercore suo [in their dung], rest above all on deriving the word from the root גרף, in so far as it denotes to sweep away, because dung is swept away from under the cattle, or out of their stalls.

These Chaldee words are more correctly rendered in Latin in the Polyglot Bibles thus: the wine-jars have rotted under their lids. This interpretation is confirmed by the authority of Abu Walid, the most learned grammarian of the Hebrews, cited by Ed. Pococke here as often (p. 80), who explains the words of the Chaldee translator thus: خبجت دنان الخمر وعفنت من طول مكثها فارغة [khabijat dinān al-khamr wa-ʿafinat min ṭūl makthihā fārigha] the wine-jars stink, or become rancid and musty, because they remain empty so long. It is clear that the Chaldee translator took the verb עבש in the sense of growing musty, rotting, which belongs to the Chaldee עפש, cognate in sound. The other Hebrew words, however, which he seems not to have understood well enough, he rendered by a free paraphrase.

ܥܒܫ ܥܓܠܬܐ ܥܠ ܐܘܪܝܘܬܗܝܢ, words which the Latin translator in the Polyglots renders thus: the heifers remained unfed at their mangers. But Ed. Pococke, p. 80. 82, notes that the verb ܥܒܫ is more correctly rendered they are parched or scorched, so that the more usual meaning of the Syriac ܥܒܫ is retained, and that the Syriac translator expressed the notion of being dry, which belongs to the Arabic عبس [ʿabasa], agreeing in spelling and sound with the Hebrew עבש. Cf. our note 11 below. That parched or dried-up heifers are heifers wasted by hunger scarcely needs pointing out.

No one has explained the meaning of the word פרודות better, and at the same time weighed its various interpretations more carefully, than Edward Pococke in his Commentary. Since I see that it is almost neglected today and in the hands of few, though undeservedly, for it is full of solid and exquisite learning, I shall add from it what is most to the point. "From the root פרד, which among the Hebrews, Chaldeans and Arabs means to separate or to be separated, nouns can be derived that denote something single and separated from others, such as grains of corn and the seed that is sown and committed to the earth. And it is not absurd that the Hebrew noun can be taken in this sense here too, [III, 301] although its form is quite peculiar, since it is nowhere used in Holy Scripture as a substantive, nor does any other occurrence of it appear, as with the Syriac ܦܪܕܐ, which occurs in the version of the N. T. in the sense of grain or seed sown, and in the plural grains or seeds sown. Hence it appears that it was not without weighty reason rendered thus, and explained by some of the Jews as גרגרי החטה והשערה, grains of wheat and barley, or גרגרי הזרע, grains of seed, which are sown, separated and scattered over the ground; or, as Abu Walid puts it in Arabic, الحبوب المبذورات للزراعة [al-ḥubūb al-mabdhūrāt li-l-zirāʿa], grains scattered in sowing; and R. Tanchum, الحبوب المعدودة للزراعة لانها تغرق في الارض [al-ḥubūb al-maʿdūda li-l-zirāʿa li-annahā tughraq fī al-arḍ], grains prepared for sowing, so called because they are scattered over the ground. The author of the Arabic manuscript [he means the Arabic version of the O. T., which he possessed and often cites, and which he thinks was composed by R. Saadia Haggaon, in the Preface, p. 16] assigns it the same meaning and derives it from the same root, rendering it المتفردات [al-mutafarridāt] (which literally means separated), where in a special note he explains that he understands קמח אלבדאר אלדי הו קמח מפרד לם פיה זואן, seed wheat, which is separated wheat, with which no darnel is mixed, לאן כאן דאב אלנאס יבדדו אלגל מן אלקמח, because it is the custom of men to sow the choicest (or most select) of the wheat. Abarbinel too takes it so, but he also adduces the reason for the meaning, namely, not that one grain is separated and distinct from another, or set apart from darnel, but that the seed is separated (or withdrawn) from the eyes of men and hidden in the recesses of the soil. And thus all these agree in the same meaning and the same root of the noun, however much they waver somewhat in the explanation of the derivation." So Pococke.

"Abu Walid," says Pococke, pp. 84–85, "whom we judge the most ancient of the grammarians among the Jews that we possess, has خطوطها [khuṭūṭuhā], their furrows, by which he understands الخطوط التي يخطها الزارع بالسكة بعد البذر [al-khuṭūṭ allatī yakhuṭṭuhā al-zāriʿ bi-l-sikka baʿda al-badhr], those which the farmer draws with his ploughshare after the grain has been sown, which are, he adds, like خدوش في الارض [khudūsh fī al-arḍ], scratches in the ground. And to the same effect he says again in another place (under the root פרד) that they are so named تشبيها بالخدوش [tashbīhan bi-l-khudūsh], on account of their likeness to scratches or wounds made in someone's skin by the nails, which are breaks in the skin. R. Tanchum uses almost the same word, so that for him too תחת מגרפותיהם is תחת חרושהא, under their scratchings, [III, 302] i.e. تحت الخطوط التي يحفرها الحراث التي كانها كسور في الارض [taḥta al-khuṭūṭ allatī yaḥfiruhā al-ḥarrāth allatī kaʾannahā kusūr fī al-arḍ], the furrows (lines) which the plough digs, which are like ridges in the earth; just as elsewhere (Psal. LXV, 10.) they are called, on almost the same principle, גדודים, incisions (our furrows), from גדד, to cut. For this meaning they seek support from the word אגרוף, which occurs in Exod. XXI, 18., and which our people and others, both Jews and Christians, render fist, but which for them (Abu Walid under the root גרף) is شادخ كاسر [shādikh kāsir], something that wounds or makes an incision, كل يجرح او يشدخ به [kull yajraḥ aw yashdakh bihi]. Meanwhile it is evident that by these lines or scratchings (as they call them) we are to understand not hollowed and open furrows but ones covered with earth, drawn through it by the plough or harrow, since the word joined to it, תחת, under, necessarily requires this. Accordingly Aben Esra explains it by העפר, dust or earth, and Kimchi by חתיכות העפר, fragments or particles of dust; hence our people, with most of the more recent interpreters, render it clods. Some try to confirm this from the Arabic language, in which جُرْفٌ [jurf] is said to signify a clod of earth which water rolls along or carries off with it, so that it could be used for any clod. From the root of this word, Hebrew גרף and Arabic أجرف [ajrafa], which means both to roll together and to carry off or scatter, a noun could perhaps not unsuitably be derived denoting earth broken, poured over, rolled together, or thrown upon the grain by plough or harrow; the sense 'clod' being confirmed by الجرفة [al-jurfa], meaning a piece of broken bread, and so perhaps certain fragments or broken pieces of some other thing, such as clods of earth. There remains another explanation of the word, mentioned by the author of an Arabic manuscript (although he expresses it by the Hebrew word itself, مجارفهم [majārifuhum]), namely انادر [anādir], which designates either granaries or heaps of grain in granaries, التي منها يجرف القمح ويودا الي الصحرا [allatī minhā yujraf al-qamḥ wa-yūdā ilā al-ṣaḥrā], from which the wheat (or seed) is removed (or turned away, or taken away) and carried into the field to be committed to the earth, so that this root has the same notion as the preceding, namely of taking away or removing. Grotius reports that some have taken it in this way, rendering heaps, as if the seeds or grains had been spoiled and made unfit for sowing already in the heaps into which they had been gathered." — Since Arabic مِجْرَفَةٌ [mijrafa] is a mattock, or an implement of that kind, suited for throwing out dung or sweeping away dust, Michaelis in Supplemm. ad Lexx. vol. II, p. 361, holds that Hebrew מגרפה too should be taken in the same sense, and renders our words: the grains diminish under the chaff. This sense, already meagre in itself, cannot be admitted also because he takes עבש in the sense of contracting or diminishing, which it has in no cognate dialect. But much more to be rejected is the interpretation of Eckermann, who renders this clause: the things set aside (from פרד, to separate) vanished on account of the chaff (תחת, because of, on account of, as in Ierem. V, 19.), i.e. because what had been set aside in the barns was continually consumed together with the chaff.

"But either Bochart himself," says Pococke, p. 87, "is mistaken here, or the copy he uses is corrupt. For in all the copies, printed and manuscript, that I have happened to see, other words are added to those cited which complete the sense and reveal his meaning to be the contrary: after the words מפני הגשמים, because of the rains, there is added: שלא ירדו עליהם כי גם כן תהיה עצירה גדולה בשנים האלה, which will not come down upon them, for there will be a great drought (or want of rain) at that time."

But that Bochart dealt no differently with Diodati than with Kimchi is asserted by the same Pococke, loc. cit.: "It is true," he says, "that the words of his that are cited are found in the Geneva quarto edition of 1607, namely that the grains were spoiled da soverchie piogge, by excessive rain; but in the later edition (Geneva 1641, in largest format) words are found which indicate exactly the opposite, namely that they could not sprout per lestreme ioccita, because of extreme drought, as if he remained in doubt with others whether this damage or that was brought on either by the frequency of rains or by their excessive scarcity, or, as some prefer, by joining both, after long-lasting rains, a raging drought, or the heat of the sun. But Kimchi, as has been said, does not attribute it to an abundance of rain, but to a lack or want of rain."

"But that ancient grammarian Abu Walid (under the words עבש and פרד) tries to draw out the meaning of the verb עבש by comparing it with the Arabic word عبس [ʿbs], inasmuch as it means the same as يبس [yabisa], to dry up, which he judges to fit this passage best, because the damage described here seems to have been caused by drought rather than by moisture, so that the words עבשו פרודות [III, 304] mean nothing other than אלתשניע ואלהעטים לאמר אלקחט אלדי נאלהם התי יבשת אלחבוב תחת אלארץ אד לא ינזל עליהא מטר פלם תנבת, to heighten the horror and the magnitude of the famine that overwhelmed them, so that the grains dried up under the earth, because rain did not fall on them, and so they could not come up. R. TANCHUM says that this too happened through a great drought, and he thinks it can be shown from this ان مع الجراد عدم الامطار [anna maʿa al-jarād ʿadam al-amṭār] that together with the locusts there was also a lack of rain there, which also appears from what follows (vs. 20.), כי יבשו אפקי מים, the channels of the waters have dried up." Thus Pococke, loc. cit. p. 81. 87 f.
That drought favours the increase of locusts is also shown with many examples by IGNATIUS DE ASSO, pp. 9, 15, German trans.
